chief_complaint: sharp right upper quadrant abdominal pain after fatty meal with fever and vomiting
hpi_details: 47F presenting with persistent RUQ pain radiating to right shoulder, positive Murphy's sign, leukocytosis, and gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening (>4mm) on ultrasound.
ideas: She thinks she is having an extreme episode of acid indigestion or an ulcer flare-up triggered by the greasy dinner she ate.
concerns: She is worried that she will need sudden emergency surgery and have to miss her daughter's upcoming college graduation this weekend.
expectations: She hopes to receive an injection to stop the vomiting and a prescription for strong painkillers so she can recover in time for the weekend.

available_results.value: Gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign; common bile duct 5 mm

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Calculous Cholecystitis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Calculous Cholecystitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes NPO status, IV fluid resuscitation, IV antibiotics, and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 24-72 hours of symptom onset, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sharp right upper quadrant abdominal pain after fatty meal with fever and vomiting
Key HPI features: 47F presenting with persistent RUQ pain radiating to right shoulder, positive Murphy's sign, leukocytosis, and gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening (>4mm) on ultrasound.

Objective/Exam findings: Fever and RUQ tenderness with a positive Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on palpation). Labs show leukocytosis. Ultrasound demonstrates gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening (>4mm) and pericholecystic fluid.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Calculous Cholecystitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Biliary colic (pain resolves within hours, no fever) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: High fever with rigors — suggests progression to cholangitis or gangrenous gallbladder.
management_principles: Keep patient NPO, initiate IV fluid resuscitation, and administer IV analgesia and antiemetics
Start IV antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negatives and anaerobes (e.g., ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, or piperacillin-tazobactam)
Obtain General Surgery consultation for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally within 24-72 hours of symptom onset
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.objective: Fever and RUQ tenderness with a positive Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on palpation). Labs show leukocytosis. Ultrasound demonstrates gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening (>4mm) and pericholecystic fluid.
reference_soap.plan: 1. NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, IV analgesia and antiemetics. 2. IV antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negatives and anaerobes. 3. General Surgery consultation for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally within 24-72 hours of symptom onset.

learning_objectives: Elicit and interpret a positive Murphy's sign on physical exam
Distinguish acute cholecystitis from simple biliary colic based on persistence, fever, and inflammatory markers
Select ultrasound as the first-line imaging study for suspected cholecystitis
Outline pre-operative management and timing for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy

teaching.one_liner: A gallstone blocks the cystic duct, causing gallbladder inflammation with persistent RUQ pain, fever, and a positive Murphy's sign — distinct from biliary colic by its persistence and inflammation.
differentials: Biliary colic (pain resolves within hours, no fever)
red_flags: High fever with rigors — suggests progression to cholangitis or gangrenous gallbladder

must_ask.objective: Character and radiation of the pain
must_ask.say: Where is the pain, and does it spread to your right shoulder blade?
Did the pain start after eating a fatty meal?
Has the pain been constant, or does it come and go?
Have you had a fever with this pain?
Have you felt nauseated or vomited?

history.answer: I have this severe sharp pain in the right side of my upper belly that started after dinner, and I have been throwing up.
It started suddenly about eight hours ago, roughly two hours after eating dinner, and has been getting steadily worse.
The pain is in my upper right abdomen right under my ribs, and it has stayed in the same spot without moving anywhere else.
Yes, the pain shoots through to my back and up into my right shoulder blade.
It is a continuous, sharp, aching pain that stays constant rather than coming in waves.
It has been constant for the past eight hours and has not let up at all.
Right now it is an 8 out of 10, whereas it started around a 4 or 5 after dinner.
Taking a deep breath, coughing, or moving around makes it sting much worse, and lying completely still gives only slight relief.
I had mild stomach indigestion and upper belly fullness after greasy meals a few times in the past year, but it always faded in an hour and was never this painful.
I ate fried chicken and french fries for dinner with one bottle of beer about two hours before the pain began.
I felt very nauseous and vomited twice, mostly bringing up undigested dinner and bitter yellowish fluid without any blood.
I have been feeling hot and feverish with mild chills since early this morning, but I have not had violent shaking chills.
No, my eyes and skin look their normal color, and my urine and stool look normal too.
I passed gas this morning and had a normal brown bowel movement yesterday, with no diarrhea, black tarry stool, or blood.
No, peeing feels completely normal with no pain, burning, increased urgency, or blood in the urine.
No, I have not felt faint, lightheaded, or dizzy at any point.
No, I have not had any abnormal vaginal bleeding, spotting, or unusual discharge.
No chest pain or pressure, but taking a deep breath hurts my upper stomach so I have been taking shallower breaths.
I took one tablet of acetaminophen about four hours ago, but it did not relieve the pain at all, and I do not take aspirin or ibuprofen.
No, I have never had heart palpitations, irregular heart rhythms, blood clots, or blood vessel disorders.
I thought it was just really bad heartburn or an ulcer acting up after eating greasy fried food for dinner.
I'm really worried this means I'll need an emergency operation and miss my daughter's college graduation this weekend.
I do not have any chronic medical illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or liver problems.
I had an uncomplicated appendectomy when I was twenty-two, but no other operations or hospital stays.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or health supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, usually one or two glasses of wine or beer on the weekend.
I work full-time as an accountant, and I live at home with my husband and two teenage children.
My mother had gallstones and had her gallbladder removed in her fifties, and my father has treated high blood pressure.
My menstrual cycles are regular every twenty-eight days, and my last period began two weeks ago.
My husband had a vasectomy several years ago, so there is no possibility that I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 125/80 mmHg, pulse 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius.
Patient appears in acute distress, grimacing and clutching her right upper abdomen while lying still.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are clear without jaundice.
Breath sounds are vesicular and clear bilaterally without wheezing or crackles.
Heart sounds show a regular tachycardia without murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Abdomen is flat with a well-healed small scar in the right lower quadrant and no distension or discoloration.
Normoactive bowel sounds are heard throughout all four quadrants with no bruits.
Percussion is normally tympanitic throughout with no shifting dullness.
Soft abdomen with severe tenderness upon light and deep palpation localized to the right upper quadrant, without masses.
Positive Murphy sign with abrupt inspiratory arrest due to sharp pain during deep subcostal palpation.
No localized rebound tenderness or involuntary abdominal muscular guarding.
Negative McBurney point tenderness, negative Rovsing sign, and negative psoas sign.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on either flank.
